short: The telobox factors TERF1 (TRF1) and TERF2 (TRF2) bind the vertebrate telomeric repeat TTAGGG through a single Myb-type helix-turn-helix domain that is, structurally, a homeodomain-like fold. Both work as preformed homodimers, and the dimer reads two YTAGGGTTR half-sites whose spacing and orientation are almost unconstrained, so the footprint on a tandem repeat array is flexible rather than fixed. ZBTB48 (TZAP) is a zinc-finger protein that binds the same telomeric and subtelomeric variant repeats and triggers telomere trimming. Because the motif is the telomeric repeat itself, a match in the genome is almost always either a true telomere, a subtelomeric region, or an interstitial telomeric sequence - not a conventional regulatory element.
long:
## The factors

Human telomeres end in several kilobases of tandem TTAGGG repeats, bound by the six-protein shelterin
complex. Two shelterin subunits supply the double-stranded DNA contact: TERF1 (TRF1) and TERF2 (TRF2) [PMID:7502076,9326950].
Each has an N-terminal domain (acidic in TRF1, basic in TRF2), a central TRFH homodimerization domain, and
a C-terminal Myb/SANT-type helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain [PMID:7502076,9326950]. The Myb domain here is a single repeat, not
the three-repeat array of c-MYB, and crystal and NMR structures show that it adopts a homeodomain-like
fold, the same solution the budding-yeast telomere protein Rap1 uses [PMID:9739097,15608617]. Both proteins bind DNA as preformed
homodimers in which the two DNA-binding domains are independent structural units on a flexible tether [PMID:15608617,10523316]. The
family name comes from the telobox, a Myb-related telomeric DNA-binding motif recognized as a conserved
module across yeast, plants and humans [PMID:8614633].

ZBTB48, also called TZAP or HKR3, is grouped here because it binds the same sequence, but it is a
different protein class: a BTB/POZ zinc-finger factor, not a telobox protein. It binds telomeric and
subtelomeric variant repeats directly [PMID:28500257], competes with TRF1 and TRF2 for long telomeres [PMID:28082411], and also acts as a
conventional transcriptional activator at a small set of promoters [PMID:28500257]. TRF1 and TRF2 are broadly expressed [PMID:9326950]
and essential; ZBTB48 is a more transient telomere visitor.

## The motif

The literature consensus is the telomeric repeat itself, TTAGGG, and in practice the unit the protein
reads is the 7-9 bp half-site YTAGGGTTR [PMID:10523316]. High-resolution crystal structures of the TRF1 and TRF2
DNA-binding domains on telomeric DNA show that both recognize the same TAGGGTT site, that two of the three
G-C base pairs characteristic of the repeat are read specifically, and that an unusually large number of
ordered water molecules mediate the protein-DNA interface [PMID:15608617]. SELEX with dimeric TRF1 defined the site as
bipartite: two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with essentially no constraint on distance or relative orientation,
simultaneously contacted by one dimer, with the intervening DNA looped out [PMID:10523316]. A tandem repeat array
therefore does not have one canonical binding register.

The matrices in this atlas all describe fragments of this repeat in one orientation or the other: AGGGTT
(HOCOMOCO TERF1), AACCCTA (CIS-BP TERF2), TCCCTAA and GGTCCCTDA (ZBTB48/TZAP), GGTCCCT (a Vierstra ZBTB
archetype). These are the same repeat unit read on opposite strands and phased differently, which is why
the atlas medoid, TCCCTAA, looks unlike TTAGGG at first glance - it is CCCTAA, the reverse complement,
shifted by one. Family cohesion is about 0.81, and the residual spread is phase and strand, not genuine
specificity differences. None of these short matrices captures the dimeric bipartite logic, so a scan
reports individual half-sites rather than functional dimer footprints. The members are not distinguishable
from sequence: TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read the same repeat.

## Where it acts

Almost everywhere this motif occurs it is a telomeric repeat. ChIP-seq for TRF1 and TRF2 recovers
telomeres, subtelomeric regions, and a defined subset of interstitial telomeric sequences (ITSs) -
internal blocks of degenerate TTAGGG repeats scattered through the genome, many of them near or within
gene introns - plus some centromeric and pericentromeric satellite DNA [PMID:21423270]. ITSs are themselves unstable and
are recombination-prone. ZBTB48 additionally binds subtelomeric variant repeats [PMID:28500257]. So the honest description
of the genomic distribution is: chromosome ends, subtelomeres, ITSs and satellite arrays, with only a
small number of genuine promoter sites, such as the ZBTB48 target MTFP1 [PMID:28500257]. This motif is not a promoter
element in the ordinary sense, and CpG-island promoter enrichment is not expected.

## Biology and disease

TRF1 is a negative regulator of telomere length: overexpression shortens telomeres progressively and a
dominant-negative form lengthens them, in telomerase-positive cells [PMID:9034193]. TRF2 protects chromosome ends from
being processed as double-strand breaks; its inhibition causes end-to-end chromosome fusions [PMID:9476899] and triggers
an ATM-dependent damage response, and TRF2 is implicated in the t-loop structure at telomeres, although
the crystal structures show no DNA distortion that would explain that activity [PMID:15608617]. ZBTB48/TZAP binds
preferentially to long telomeres, where shelterin density is low, and initiates telomere trimming - rapid
deletion of telomeric repeats - which sets an upper limit on telomere length [PMID:28082411]; it is also a negative
regulator of telomere length in cancer cells regardless of their telomere-maintenance mechanism [PMID:28500257]. Telomere
dysfunction through these routes connects to senescence, genome instability in cancer, and the
telomere-biology disorders, and TRF1 and TRF2 are reviewed as shelterin components in that context.

## Reading a hit

The practical rule for this family is different from every other family in the atlas: a match is a
telomeric repeat, so ask where it is before asking who bound it. If the hit is at a chromosome end or in a
subtelomere, it is telomeric. If it is internal, the most likely explanation is an interstitial telomeric
sequence or a satellite array, and a TTAGGG-rich internal block will score highly whether or not any
protein binds it. Only after excluding those should a hit be read as a regulatory element. The members
cannot be separated by sequence - TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read TTAGGG - and the short matrices available
represent single half-sites rather than the flexible bipartite site a TRF dimer actually occupies, so
scores will not track dimer affinity. The CIS-BP TERF2 model is inferred from mouse Terf2 at 92%
DNA-binding-domain identity rather than measured on the human protein, the HOCOMOCO TZAP model is
ChIP-only (grade B), and the Vierstra archetype is labelled for the broad ZBTB group rather than for
ZBTB48 specifically.
caveats: This motif is the telomeric repeat, so most matches are telomeric, subtelomeric, interstitial telomeric sequence or satellite DNA rather than regulatory elements - check location before interpreting. TRF1, TRF2 and ZBTB48 all read the same TTAGGG repeat and cannot be separated by sequence. The available matrices (6-9 bp fragments in both orientations; the medoid TCCCTAA is the reverse complement, phase shifted) capture single half-sites, whereas TRF dimers bind two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with almost no spacing or orientation constraint, so scores do not track real affinity. The CIS-BP TERF2 model is inferred from mouse Terf2 (92% DBD identity), the HOCOMOCO TZAP model is ChIP-only at grade B, and the Vierstra archetype is labelled for ZBTB generally.

timeline.finding: A nuclear activity, TRF, is found in human, mouse and monkey cells that binds duplex TTAGGG repeat arrays but not closely related repeats such as TTGGGG or TTAGGC.
timeline.methods: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays with nuclear extracts
timeline.open: The protein behind the activity was unidentified.

timeline.finding: TRF (later TRF1) is cloned as a telomeric protein with one Myb-type DNA-binding repeat that colocalizes with telomeric DNA in interphase and at metaphase chromosome ends.
timeline.methods: Protein purification and cDNA cloning; immunofluorescence

timeline.finding: The telobox is defined as a Myb-related telomeric DNA-binding motif shared by yeast Tbf1, several plant proteins and human TRF and a second human protein.
timeline.methods: Deletion mapping; sequence comparison; DNA-binding assays

timeline.finding: TRF2 is cloned as a distant TRF1 homologue with a very similar Myb-related domain that also binds duplex TTAGGG; the two proteins exist predominantly as separate homodimers.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; in vitro binding; dimerization assays; metaphase localization
timeline.open: Why two proteins read one repeat, and whether they discriminate between sites, was unknown.

timeline.finding: SELEX with dimeric TRF1 reveals a bipartite site of two YTAGGGTTR half-sites with no constraint on spacing or orientation, contacted simultaneously by one dimer with the intervening DNA looped out.
timeline.methods: SELEX; binding affinities; DNase I footprinting; electron microscopy

timeline.finding: Crystal structures of the TRF1 and TRF2 DNA-binding domains on telomeric DNA show both recognize the same TAGGGTT site through homeodomain-like folds, reading two of the three G-C pairs, with many water-mediated contacts.
timeline.open: No DNA distortion was seen that would explain TRF2's proposed role in t-loop formation.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide ChIP-seq maps TRF1 and TRF2 beyond telomeres to a subset of interstitial telomeric sequences and to centromeric and pericentromeric satellites, often near genes or in introns.
timeline.open: Whether these extratelomeric sites have regulatory function was not tested.

timeline.finding: Two groups characterize ZBTB48 (TZAP) as a C2H2 zinc-finger protein that binds telomeric and subtelomeric variant repeats directly, prefers long telomeres with low shelterin, triggers telomere trimming, and also activates a small set of genes including MTFP1.
timeline.methods: Telomere-binding protein screens; ChIP-seq; RNA-seq; telomere-length assays

open: How TRF2 promotes t-loop formation is unexplained: TRF2 is implicated in t-loops, but its DNA-binding domain does not distort the duplex in crystal structures, so the activity must come from other parts of the protein or complex.

Whether TRF1 and TRF2 binding at interstitial telomeric sequences and satellites has a regulatory role is unsettled: ChIP-seq places them at a subset of such sites, often near genes or within introns, and a role in long-range chromosome organization and gene regulation has been proposed but not demonstrated.
